In this presentation, I introduce Assignment Seven for the Software Artifacts Laboratory: a multi-model evaluation of the scientific software artifact called K-Agent, associated with the 2026 Brazilian Symposium on Computer Networks and Distributed Systems, or SBRC. The objective was to compare assessments by three language models from different providers, using two criteria: functionality and reproducibility. We also examined practical execution evidence, without confusing our academic assessment with the official artifact badges.

The evaluation followed two historical stages. First, each model reviewed the repository documentation under the SBRC evaluation guidelines. Second, the models received the same summary of execution logs: the random selection method ran successfully, whereas an earlier K-Agent attempt failed to connect to the Ollama service. The models then revised their judgments. Importantly, they only reviewed reported logs; none of the three language models executed the software. Independent experiments were conducted later in GitHub Codespaces, and those results must be considered separately.

The F badge stands for functional. Supporting it requires observable software execution and verifiable outputs. The R badge stands for reproducible, which demands stronger evidence: repeating key experiments and comparing the outcomes against the scientific results claimed in the paper. Running a reduced experiment is not the same as reproducing every published result. The official SBRC 2026 committee awarded both F and R badges to the original artifact. Our classroom exercise does not revoke or change those awards.

Starting with GPT Six, from OpenAI: in the document-based review, functionality received a favorable assessment with reservations, whereas reproducibility was rated partial. After receiving the historical connection-error log, the model changed its functionality assessment to partial and kept reproducibility as partial. This reflects caution when execution evidence is incomplete. Here, the term partial describes an AI-generated assessment. It is not an official category of artifact badge used by the symposium.

Claude, from Anthropic, was cautious from the beginning. In its document-based assessment, it regarded both functionality and reproducibility as only partially supported. It highlighted risks involving documentation and dependency configuration. After receiving the execution summary, it maintained both partial assessments and emphasized an additional risk to reproducibility. These concerns do not, by themselves, demonstrate a defect in the algorithm.

Gemini, from Google, gave a more favorable evaluation. During the documentary stage, it recommended both the F and R badges. Even after receiving the same historical logs, Gemini maintained its positive recommendation for both badges, although it added a reservation regarding reproducibility. This difference from GPT Six and Claude illustrates how language models may demand different levels of evidence before making the same recommendation. A model's judgment cannot replace hands-on technical verification.

Now let us examine the later practical evidence. In Codespaces, running Python version three point ten, the random selection baseline completed one training round and saved its model. A subsequent reduced K-Agent test involved five clients and two rounds, using the Flower framework and the Qwen Three language model through Ollama. The chat interface returned HTTP status two hundred. The Oort client-selection tool was invoked, one client was selected for training, and the process finished with exit code zero. These observations demonstrate that the core K-Agent workflow operated in this limited environment. Crucially, the three language models did not receive this later test as part of their earlier evaluation.

When comparing the judgments after the same historical logs, we observe a clear disagreement. GPT Six and Claude retained partial evaluations, whereas Gemini continued to recommend the badges, with a reservation concerning R. None of the three models independently reproduced the principal scientific metrics. A refused connection indicates a problem in that particular environment; it does not prove that the algorithm is generally defective. Conversely, succeeding in two training rounds does not establish that every published experiment has been reproduced.

In conclusion, this assignment achieved its objective of comparing three models from three providers and examining how documentary judgments relate to execution evidence. The later test strengthened the evidence that the K-Agent software is functional. However, we did not fully reproduce the quantitative experiments or verify the traffic reduction reported in the paper. Fifty training rounds were not required by the class assignment, although running larger experiments would be relevant for verifying that particular research claim. The central lesson is to use language models as supporting reviewers, alongside explicit criteria, execution logs, and human validation. The official F and R badges awarded by SBRC remain unchanged.
